title: Practice problems and live demos
idea: Good LLD interview practice means solving graded problems under a 45-minute clock, then demoing each design with checks that cover its edge cases.
points: Think aloud: state each assumption and trade-off at the moment you make it.
Climb the levels in order; beat the 45-minute clock on warm-ups before concurrency.
Demo with named checks for ties, limits and bad input, beyond the happy path.
After each mock, list what you skipped; that list is your next practice session.

hero.caption: Move up a level once you finish a problem from it in 45 minutes, with a running demo.

code.title: Happy-path demo
code.caption: A leaderboard demo that only shows the happy path. One interviewer question exposes the bug.

walk.text: Three distinct scores, top two printed. The output looks right, so the candidate moves on.
The interviewer asks about a tie. A second player scores 90.
The design keys a `TreeMap` by score. Keys are unique, so it can hold one player per score.
`put` on an existing key replaces the value. The earlier player at 90 vanishes without an error.
Four players recorded, fewer counted. A demo with a tie check would have caught this in minute one.

code.title: Demo as checks
code.caption: The fixed design, demoed as named checks. Each line answers a question the interviewer would ask.

walk.text: Each check names one edge case: ties, tie order, oversized k, an update and two bad inputs.
A small runner prints PASS or FAIL. No JUnit is needed in an interview editor.
The map is keyed by player, the true identity. Equal scores can no longer collide.
`record` rejects a null player and a negative score before touching state.
`top` sorts by score descending, then name, so ties have a fixed, explainable order.
The final count gives a one-line verdict the interviewer can read at a glance.

pitfalls: Memorising one parking-lot answer; a changed requirement shows you cannot adapt it.
Demoing only the happy path; ties, empty input and limits are where bugs hide.
Keying a map by a value that can repeat, such as a score; entries silently overwrite.

quiz.why: Keys in a `TreeMap` are unique. The second `put` with key 90 replaces the value, so two keys remain and 90 maps to dee.

takeaway: Practise by level, under a clock, and demo the edge cases.
